what_it_does: This paper describes a complete integrated circuit (SoC—a system on a chip) for a high-end neural prosthetic (a robotic limb or sensory device controlled by brain signals). A key innovation is closed-loop sensory feedback: the chip not only reads neural signals from the brain and stimulates muscles, but it also sends tactile information back to the brain so the user can actually feel what they're touching—just like a natural limb. The chip uses frequency-splitting for wireless power and data (sending power on one radio frequency, data on another to avoid interference). To minimize power, it compresses the neural data stream using on-chip unsupervised learning (grouping similar neural spike patterns without pre-training), and a noise-rejection circuit prevents the stimulation signals from being misread as feedback. The result: neural data streams at 200 megabits/second while using only 0.67 picojoules per bit—exceptionally efficient for an implanted device.
